title: Gaitskill Mound's engraved tablets
summary: In Montgomery County, Gaitskill Mound is an earthwork built by Adena people, a mound listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1975.
bodyMarkdown:
In Montgomery County stands Gaitskill Mound, an earthwork far older than the county's towns. The [Kentucky Historical Society marker for the Gaitskill Mound](https://history.ky.gov/markers/the-gaitskill-mound) (No. 1655) identifies it as an Indian mound built by Adena people. The marker gives their time in the Ohio Valley as about 800 B.C. to A.D. 700. The mound was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1975.

## The Adena people

The marker describes the Adena as people who began cultivating simple crops, which created a mixed economy of hunting and farming. "Central to Adena life," it says, "were rituals involving cremation and mound building."

Other sources draw the Adena era differently. [Grokipedia's Adena culture article](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture) dates the culture to about 600 BCE to 100 CE and notes that chronologies vary by region and source. It describes small, mobile communities in the central and upper Ohio Valley that supplemented hunting and gathering with crops such as goosefoot, sunflower and squash.

Adena people are known above all for conical burial mounds and for circular earthworks used as ceremonial centers. In Kentucky's Bluegrass region, Adena sites show shared ritual practices.

## How the tablets told the story

According to the marker, engraved stone tablets found at the Gaitskill Mound show that it is an Adena mound. The marker does not say when the tablets were found, who found them or where they are now.

[The survey's Gaitskill/Wright Mounds page](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Wright-Mounds.aspx) explains why such tablets are telling. Such tablets are small, flat rectangles of stone, about the size of a palm, cut from shale, limestone, siltstone or fine sandstone. They engraved them with distinctive designs, often highly stylized wild turkeys or birds of prey. In the survey's reading, the designs may picture a world in layers, with the earth hanging between a sky realm above and a watery underworld below.

Just one of them, from the [Wright Mounds](/stories/wright-mounds-montgomery-county/) elsewhere in Montgomery County, was found by archaeologists during an excavation.

What the tablets were used for is still debated. Paint has been found on some tablets of the [Adena culture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture). That has led archaeologists to propose that they were used to stamp designs on cloth, hides or skin, possibly as outlines for tattoos.

## Kentucky today

Montgomery County's Adena heritage shaped the name of its county seat. [Grokipedia's Mount Sterling article](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mount_Sterling,_Kentucky) describes another large Adena mound, about 25 feet high and 125 feet across, at what is now Queen and Locust streets. It held artifacts such as shell necklaces and copper beads. The settlement was first called Little Mountain Town after that mound.

It was established in 1792 and took its permanent name from Stirling, the Scottish hometown of founder Hugh Forbes. For another Adena site in northeastern Kentucky, see [Ashland's Adena mounds](/stories/ashlands-adena-mounds/).
